analysis.title: Global Economic Weekly: The fog of war
key_insights: Markets are struggling to trade several macro themes at once, which BofA says can create significant mispricing. Core PCE came in softer than expected, and Fed officials sounded dovish.

The October Fed hike probability fell from 70% to about 30% after the soft core PCE and comments from a couple of Fed officials that the Fed can wait until December. BofA argues the underlying fundamentals still point to higher rates.

BofA's base case: (1) higher global real rates remain the path of least resistance, (2) without fiscal consolidation, government intervention in financial markets is increasingly likely, (3) the Middle East conflict is far from over, (4) US consumption and investment stay strong as long as the AI trade does not break.

Long-term real rates are explained by a higher r* (the equilibrium real rate): global private savings are not enough to finance higher global investment at the prevailing rate. An unchanged policy stance therefore amounts to looser financial conditions, which forces the market to reprice and the Fed to tighten.
BofA says fundamentals drive both the long end of the curve and the Fed's reaction function. Short- and long-term rates are correlated because they share a common factor, r*.
If the Fed skips October, it would be the third time in recent history that a hiking cycle was interrupted that early. In those episodes inflation was far below current levels.

BofA says it seems too early to interrupt the hiking cycle. It sees little to be learned by December that would raise confidence that the economy needs higher rates, and it questions whether Chair Warsh can justify waiting with core PCE persistently around 3%, right before the midterm elections.

Brent trades above $100 per barrel despite reports that Middle East oil flows are normalizing. Each de-escalation drops the price toward a higher floor, which BofA attributes to inventory depletion and less credible de-escalation attempts.
Refinery impairment and rising diesel and fertilizer prices keep upside inflation risks intact. BofA cannot rule out conflict escalation ahead of the US midterms.

BofA argues that by not reacting to a sequence of supply shocks, the Fed passively eases policy by validating lower real rates. Oil price volatility itself can be inflationary because prices are sticky downward, which adds an argument for a more hawkish stance.

US: BEA methodology changes to portfolio management and investment advice, computer and software accessories, and legal services lowered recent inflation. July core PCE was revised down by 35bp to 3.0% y/y, and the September reading was also 3.0%.

BofA still estimates underlying US inflation at 2.5% y/y with little sign of improvement over 12 months. It expects the Fed to take a risk-management approach and tighten at its remaining two meetings this year.
Inflation risks are tilted to the upside from AI demand, energy, pockets of labor tightness and resilient consumer demand. The FOMC is nearly unanimous that risks to core PCE are skewed upward.

Hyperscaler capex is projected to rise about 90% y/y this year and a further 36% next year. BofA expects limited direct inflation impact because electrical equipment, computers and electronic products are a small share of consumption.

Energy shortages tied to Iran and Russia-Ukraine have lifted headline inflation through gasoline and core inflation through airfares. Transportation services are about 0.7% of consumption and petroleum and coal products another 1.2%, which limits pass-through.

Labor market: the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio is near 1.0, quit rates are well below their 2021-23 highs and wage growth is moderating. Data center and AI-linked industries have faster wage growth than the private sector, and aging demographics and tighter immigration constrain labor supply.

Euro Area: the ECB has backstops. Short-term rates are the tool for overly tight financial conditions, and the balance sheet is for disorderly moves in spreads or long-term rates. Verbal intervention has started, and the ECB's pain threshold tends to be higher than the market's.

UK: this week's policy announcements have little near-term impact, with major changes pushed until after an election. Pension triple-lock reform offers limited near-term savings, and EU/UK progress is likely to be slow.

Asia: strong El Niño events have historically hit rice yields, but policy interventions to curb rice trade have driven prices more. South and Southeast Asia are at risk, with about 58% of global rice production and about 80% of exports.
Hungary: the NBH held at 5.50% and cut its CPI target to 2.5% from Jan-2028, the first concrete official step toward EUR adoption. It also signaled comfort with continued HUF appreciation.
Peru: BofA keeps a bullish, out-of-consensus GDP growth view on private investment and external accounts. It sees El Niño as a temporary shock and disagrees that the government is weak.

macro_indicators.interpretation: BEA methodology changes revised July down by 35bp. BofA says this lowers the measured level but not underlying inflation.
The print was softer than expected and led the market to cut October hike odds, while BofA calls it persistently high.
This is BofA's own estimate, with little evidence of improvement over 12 months. It supports the view that the Fed keeps tightening.
The market repriced after the soft core PCE and dovish Fed comments. BofA thinks skipping October is premature.
Oil is holding a higher floor despite reports of normalizing flows, which keeps upside inflation risk intact.
Held unchanged. The CPI target was cut to 2.5% from Jan-2028 as a step toward EUR adoption.
A sizeable demand shock with limited direct inflation pass-through absent supply constraints.

risk_factors: Inflation upside from AI demand, energy, labor tightness and strong consumer growth.
Fed credibility cost if it skips October with core PCE around 3% before the midterms.
Middle East escalation ahead of the US midterms, and persistent diesel, fertilizer and refinery disruption.
A break in the AI trade would undermine US consumption and investment.
Government intervention in financial markets without fiscal consolidation.
Disorderly spread or long-term rate moves in the euro area.
El Niño and rice trade restrictions in South and Southeast Asia.

vol_and_positioning: Fed pricing: October hike probability fell from 70% to about 30% after the soft core PCE and dovish Fed comments.
BofA says markets reprice hikes in direct proportion to oil shocks, but oil volatility may be what matters for policy.
geopolitical: Middle East/Iran war: oil flows may be normalizing, but Brent stays above $100, and BofA says the conflict is far from ending and escalation before the US midterms cannot be ruled out.
Russia-Ukraine conflict: cited with Iran as a source of persistent energy and refined product shortages.
UK/EU: a closer relationship could deliver growth dividends, but serious negotiations are unlikely until after an election.

tension_points.bull_case: Dovish Fed officials and the soft core PCE support waiting until December, and the market cut October odds to about 30%.
tension_points.bear_case: BofA says it is too early to interrupt the cycle. Core PCE is persistently near 3%, underlying inflation is 2.5%, and energy is an upside risk.
tension_points.what_invalidates: BofA says little can be learned between October and December to raise confidence that the economy needs higher rates, so a hold in October would not be justified by incoming data.

tension_points.bull_case: Reports suggest oil flows from the Middle East are normalizing, even though transportation costs are higher.
tension_points.bear_case: Brent stays above $100, and each de-escalation falls toward a higher floor. Refinery impairment and rising diesel and fertilizer prices keep inflation risk up.

theme_stances.key_argument: Underlying inflation is 2.5% and risks are tilted up, so the Fed should tighten at its remaining two meetings this year.
theme_stances.evidence: too early to interrupt the hiking cycle

theme_stances.key_argument: Global savings are insufficient to finance higher investment at prevailing rates, which raises r*.
theme_stances.evidence: higher global real rates is still the path of least resistance

theme_stances.key_argument: Private investment and external accounts support growth, and El Niño is a temporary shock.
theme_stances.evidence: bullish, out-of-consensus view on GDP growth
